newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey hopes $10 billion from new revenue package.
newsitem.headline: Turkey hopes $10 billion from new revenue package.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan said he would present on Thursday the government's second big revenue-raising package in two months, aimed at generating $10 billion to plug deficits.
"Preparations for the second package are complete," Erbakan told reporters before a meeting on Wednesday with senior economy officials.
"It will be presented to the public tomorrow after a final review," he said.

The package is expected to contain short-term privatisation plans, securitisation of state real estate, sale of state property and a central cash management system to "pool" public revenues in a single account to help poor state firms.
Erbakan later told reporters the state Etibank would be given priority in the government's slow privatisation drive.
"I am hoping that the cabinet meeting tonight will come out with a decision to privatise Etibank ," he said. "Later some 30 other state companies will be sold off in line with a calendar."

Analysts said the short-term privatisation plans of the package could also include the sale of generalised system for mobiles (GSM) licences by Turk Telekom as the first part of its sell-off plan, and tenders for lucrative industrial plants.

The first package, disclosed on July 31, included speedy privatisation, issuing foreign-currency denominated bonds, sale of state property, incentives and tax exemptions for Turkish workers abroad to channel their savings into the country and a six-percent charge on the financing of some imports.

The Islamist-led government aims to raise $10 billion from each of the two packages in the next three years. The government expects a budget deficit of 1,300 trillion lira ($14.4 billion) this year, up from a target of 800 trillion lira.
The first package has failed to fuel optimism in the business community and markets which saw it as unrealistic and impractical.

"Anything concrete about the cash pool might be interesting. But the second package is played down in the market because they failed to implement the first one," said Ali Ozenc, assistant treasurer at private Finansbank.
Nalan Erkarakas of Kentbank said: "What is important for the market is the putting into practice of the package rather than its contents."
On Friday, the treasury collected offers by Turkish banks for $1.12 billion worth of three-year foreign currency denominated bonds with September 25 value date as part of the first package.
The stock market index has surged 4.5 percent since Friday partly due to lower yields in this week's t-bill auction after last week's foreign currency denominated bond issue.

The foreign currency denominated debt plan, outlined in the first package, aims to extend domestic debt maturities and relieve the burden of heavy borrowing in Turkish lira and at yields sharply above inflation.
The central cash management plan aims to help overcome the financial bottleneck in several public companies and institutions like social security system (SSK) and loss-making state companies.
Under the plan, a state company which needs cash will be able to draw money from the common pool instead of resorting to the treasury's borrowed funds.

Profit-making state companies such as Turk Telekom, petrochemicals producer Petkim and petroleum marketer Petrol Ofisi, and almost all state banks have been investing large sums of their idle money in repo.
Erbakan said on Tuesday the government payments to private entities would be made through cheques that would be cashed in the "central pool."

"Under the new system, surplus money from the revenues of one government institution will be used by another which is in need of money," he said. "The aim is to eliminate the government's need to borrow."
Erbakan said the government also planned additional pay rises for senior bureaucrats, security forces, academicians and judges.
The government had awarded a more-than-expected 50 percent pay rise to some seven million civil servants for the second half of 1996 soon after it won a parliamentary vote of confidence on July 8.
Analysts saw the pay rises as a populist move likely to fuel annual inflation already running at around 80 percent.
